2. Queue Length & Waiting Time Analysis

Wait times are the most visible indicator of customer experience. This section examines how queues form across time slots, location types, traffic conditions, and vehicle categories to identify where operational improvements will have the greatest impact.

Takeaway: Peak-hour waits are significantly higher across all location types, and High traffic density amplifies queue lengths. Highway stations during Peak periods show the worst wait times. Buses experience the longest average waits, likely due to longer charging sessions blocking chargers. Targeted capacity expansion at the worst-performing stations during Peak hours would have the greatest impact on customer experience.

3. Energy Consumption & Grid Load Patterns

Understanding how energy consumption and grid load vary by time and location is essential for grid stability and capacity planning. This section profiles load patterns across the network.

Takeaway: Highway stations consume more energy per session, especially during Peak hours, placing higher stress on local grids. Station load and queue length show a positive correlation — heavily loaded stations tend to accumulate longer queues. Low-power chargers (7-15 kW) handle the majority of sessions, creating a bottleneck for high-capacity vehicles like Buses.

6. Optimization Insights & Recommendations

This section synthesizes findings from all prior analyses into specific, actionable interventions. The optimization reward metric serves as a composite signal — sessions with higher rewards indicate better alignment with grid-friendly conditions.

Key Correlations

Optimization Reward by Traffic & Time Slot

Recommendations

1. Load Shifting to Off-Peak Windows Peak-hour station loads are significantly higher than Off-Peak, and optimization rewards are consistently better during Off-Peak periods. Implement time-of-use pricing incentives (e.g., 15-20% discounts for Off-Peak sessions) to shift discretionary charging away from Peak windows. Based on the data, Off-Peak sessions already show higher renewable ratios, so load shifting simultaneously improves sustainability.
2. Green Charging Incentives During Clear Weather Renewable energy ratios are highest during Clear weather (averaging 35.7% vs. 35.4% during Rainy conditions). Offer "Green Charging" pricing discounts during high-renewable windows to encourage drivers to charge when the grid is cleanest. This also improves optimization rewards, as the data shows a positive correlation between renewable quartile and reward levels.
3. Queue Management at High-Wait Stations The top 10 worst-performing stations for wait times are concentrated in Peak periods. Deploy real-time queue monitoring and dynamic charger allocation at these stations. Consider adding fast-charging capacity (50 kW+) at Highway stations during Peak hours, where Buses and Cars face the longest waits. The correlation analysis shows station load and queue length are positively linked — capping concurrent high-power sessions can prevent cascade delays.
4. Vehicle-Aware Priority Scheduling Buses occupy chargers 3-4x longer than Two-Wheelers but are not consistently prioritized. Implement a scheduling algorithm that: (a) prioritizes quick-turnaround vehicles (Two-Wheelers, Cars) during Peak to maximize throughput, and (b) allocates dedicated high-power chargers for Buses during Off-Peak. This can reduce average queue times without requiring additional hardware.
5. Dynamic Pricing Based on Grid Stress The data shows electricity prices already vary by time slot, but the optimization reward remains negative, indicating prices may not fully reflect grid conditions. Enhance dynamic pricing to factor in real-time station load and renewable availability. When station loads exceed 70 kW and renewable ratios drop below 25%, prices should rise to discourage charging; conversely, offer discounts when load is low and renewables are high.
6. Infrastructure Expansion at Bottleneck Stations Stations with the highest average demand (>70 kWh avg demand) are exclusively Highway-located and experience the worst queue lengths. Prioritize capacity expansion at these stations — either by adding charger units or upgrading existing low-power chargers to medium/high power. The prevalence of 7-15 kW chargers handling high-demand vehicles creates avoidable bottlenecks.
